#: plex collector: five JSON documents from the Plex Media Server API, keyed by the path each answers (root, status-sessions, library-sections, and one library-sections-<key>-all per section). seerr contributes nothing — the `requests` collection has no capture and cannot have one in a lab, see NAMED_RESIDUALS.
#credential: The token is an X-Plex-Token HEADER and reaches no document. This capture's token was a placeholder rather than a real one: the server was UNCLAIMED, and an unclaimed Plex grants unauthenticated access to its own subnet, which is how its setup wizard works. `myPlexSigninState: none` and `myPlexSubscription: false` in the root document are the server saying so itself.
#identity: Three members are per-instance identities and are substituted rather than bounded, because they are identities on EVERY Plex and not merely on a real one. `friendlyName` is the server's name — here docker's random container hostname, on a deployed server the operator's own word for it. `machineIdentifier` is the server's permanent id, the value plex.tv keys an account's server list on. The library `uuid`/`librarySectionUUID` pair identifies a section across renames. Classifying these by what they ARE, rather than by how harmless this particular lab instance's happen to be, is what makes the next capture safe by default instead of safe by somebody remembering.
#nothing: The bulk of the root document is capability advertising and build constants: thirty booleans naming what this build can transcode and host, the API version, the release, the platform tuple, the transcoder's bitrate/quality/resolution ladders, the streaming-brain versions, and `ownerFeatures` — a fixed list of feature GUIDs identical on every server of this release. None correlates one machine across two captures and none is a word an operator chose.
#ownerFeatures: Called out because it LOOKS like the most identifying string in the capture and is the least. It is a comma-joined list of ~60 feature GUIDs plus a few named flags; the GUIDs are Plex's own feature catalogue, byte-identical on every server running this release, and they enumerate what the SOFTWARE offers rather than anything about this install or its owner. An unclaimed server with no subscription publishes the same list as any other.
#stock-titles: THE BOUND. `Directory.*.title` (the library names), `librarySectionTitle`, `title1` and `title2` are `nothing` HERE because this lab's two libraries are called `Movies` and `TV Shows` — the stock names Plex itself proposes — over media the capture generated. On a deployed server a library title is a word the operator chose and can be genuinely revealing; it is `content` the moment a capture comes from one, and this entry must be revisited before such a capture is scrubbed. Same shape as bazarr.json's `#paths` bound.
#paths: `Location.*.path` is the media root as the SERVER sees it, which here is `/media/Movies` inside the container — the capture's own bind, locating nothing. A native install reports the operator's real media tree, which is `location`, so this is the second half of the bound above. `art`, `thumb` and `mediaTagPrefix` are different: those are paths INSIDE Plex's own bundle (`/:/resources/movie.png`), constants of the release.
#timestamps: `updatedAt`, `createdAt`, `scannedAt`, `contentChangedAt` and `mediaTagVersion` are epoch seconds. They say when this lab's libraries were made, minutes before the capture, and correlate nothing across captures — the same test bazarr.json applies to start_time.
#sessions: The sessions document carries `size` and nothing else, because nothing was playing. A session that IS playing carries the item's title, the WATCHER'S USERNAME and their player — content and identity both — and no entry here classifies any of it, deliberately: a capture with a live session cannot be scrubbed against this manifest and will be refused leaf by leaf, which is the correct outcome for a document naming a person and what they were watching.
